834.t: Choppy and Dumb, 9/11 and humor in his music
834.s: The piece evokes dread after 9/11, plays on deliberately dumb sound, and he welcomes laughter.
834.q: That’s great. Good listening. I wanted something literally to be like the sort of feeling of kind of like dread. Basically a lot of that’s about looking back a few years at 9/11, New York City. And not that particular track, but some of them were. And oh my God we have kids now, and we’re getting…

834.t: Hypothetical commission for the January 6 anniversary
834.s: He would accept, thinking of Shostakovich and Mingus mockery, depending on the political climate.
834.ch: Writing for horn, politics and creativity
834.q: Oh boy. Wow. I think I would accept it but it would be a difficult job. It would be a lot of I don't know what it would come out sounding like. Irony? Like Shostakovich type mocking of stupidity you know? Mingus? Like “Fables of Faubus.” That’s the first thing that comes to mind. Shostakovich…

136.s: A priest commissioned a Hiroshima piece; a photograph of a smiling young woman made her decide it should be about hope.
136.q: Yeah, you‟re talking about the Hiroshima piece. Well, that was commissioned by a priest—who was here not too long ago, in New York, with his son—but anyway, he‟s a jazz fan. He has quite many, he‟s very aware of my music that I have written, uh, “Minamata.” That‟s why he asked me. It was 1999 and I…

136.t: Premiere in Hiroshima, 9/11 and her important compositions
136.s: She premiered it August 6, 2001, plays 'Hope' since 9/11, and names her key works.
136.q: I thought, “Well, this is a piece of hope, so I‟d like to play it in the 21st century,” and I said, I started writing in 1998, so…. And uh, so we did: 21st [century], 2001, August 6, in Hiroshima. Then we had a little tour after that—maybe five or six concerts—then came back to the United States,…

639.t: 'Congo Square' and the mood Wiggs intended
639.s: Wiggs says he composed 'Congo Square' to evoke slaves singing there.
639.ch: Callers: Papa John Joseph to Congo Square
639.q: Well, you know, we all have metal pictures of music. Actually, what I had in mind when I put that thing on paper was to give a bit of the color, which I supposed imagined took place in Congo Square when the people used to permit the slaves to go out and sing their beautiful slave songs in Congo…

535.t: Covid Zoom sessions and weekly livestreams
535.s: During Covid he played over Zoom with musicians abroad and has done livestreams of 309 of his tunes.
535.q: Yes. It inspires me to compose. One of the things that I’ve done, and you asked me at the beginning about Covid. When Covid first started I was getting on Zoom and I was playing with a drummer from Germany, a bass player from Malmo, Sweden, a piano player from Newton, right outside of Boston. And…

578.t: How music conveys meaning; imagining a piece on January 6th
578.s: Discussion of programme notes and abstract music, then how he would musically treat January 6th, 2021.
578.q: Yes. It wouldn’t be this. It would be more like this [plays piano] and on and on it would go. And it would be very disturbing and I can see people breaking in and here everybody’s mentioned the very decent police that tried to protect the people inside the buildings. And one had a heart attack, and…

394.t: Coltrane's 'Alabama' as inspiration for turning darkness into art
394.s: 'Cry' is inspired by the ethos of Coltrane's 'Alabama': turning struggle into an expression of hope.
394.q: Yeah. Because of the story as well, and his reason for writing “Alabama” which is absolutely heart-wrenching, heartbreakingly awful and through that comes this extraordinarily beautiful expression of one man, one man and his band, and that to me is also perhaps the value of really the way of being…

1021.t: 'Here We Go', a song about war
1021.s: He wrote 'Here We Go' after 9/11 as a reaction to constant war.
1021.q: “Here We Go.” And it was my — it seems like my entire lifetime we have been at war with somebody. And after 9/11 I don’t know, one day it just occurred to me, oh here we go again. Obviously we didn’t ask for that. But I just thought wow, here we go and we don’t really know what we’re getting into…

585.s: She hopes to play certain places and projects, facing rejection, and mentions her tune 'You're the One I Think I've Waited For'.
585.q: There’s places I want to play and people I want to play with. You know I focus on it at different times. This is a quieter month for me so I’ll explore that again. I sense some — you know you’ve got to be prepared when you’re in this business for the rejection too. I might want to play at this…

415.s: He hopes to commission Elvis Costello, who writes for the Brodsky Quartet.
415.q: Yeah. In fact if people ask me now, I did an interview with the Jazz Times recently and they said, “what would you call yourself?” I guess the thing that I would call myself is an interpreter of songs, or an interpreter of material. That’s what I would call myself. I just try to filter my own…

328.t: New commissions: Africa suite for Chicago Jazz Ensemble
328.ch: Dizzy's legacy, Latin rhythm and closing
328.q: No, this was all original music I did. Last year I did a suite to Africa for the Chicago Jazz Ensemble. They asked me to do some music based on the African energy. It didn’t have to be like the music that goes on in Africa, but it had to be about what I feel about Africa.

111.s: He recalls Trane writing and playing 'Alabama' after the church bombing.
111.q: Well he wrote that after those kids got bombed in that church, that’s why he wrote that. The next day he was playing it. I said, “Oh boy” I just had tears running down my face.

589.t: Commission and research for Proclamation of Hope
589.s: Ravinia's Welz Kauffman commissioned an evening-length Lincoln work for 23 horns and vocalist Dee Alexander, with help from Guthrie Ramsey.
589.q: Yes. The Ravinia Festival, being in the state of Illinois, and Abraham Lincoln of course spent a lot of time in the state of Illinois, although he wasn’t born here, but he spent a lot of time in the state. Celebrating the anniversary of his 200th birthday, the whole state was doing things, Chicago…

408.t: What he's listening to; songwriting and lyrics
408.s: He now stays home and composes songs with his own lyrics.
408.q: Well, I’m listening to, I love the Spanish I love what the Spanish are doing, the Nuevo flamenco. But anything special? No. I’m just listening to everything, everything I can. I mean, I’ve done all the research I could possibly do. My life is no longer a chemistry set. I mean, I’m not looking to…

374.t: It's About Time, its title and commissions
374.s: Russell explains the title It's About Time, commissioned by Bosse Broberg and the Arts Council of Great Britain and premiered in Stockholm.
374.ch: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
374.q: I’d reached a point in life when that title suited it. It was about time for various things to happen in the world and in regards to myself. That’s it. It’s about time. It fits a lot of situations.

553.s: Description of the suite for quartet and orchestra, its movements about slavery, the Middle Passage, the Great Awakening and Freedom.
553.q: Yeah. I, I think it was 1992 that I did for a quartet and orchestra. The quartet being Eternal Winds, which features Adam Rudolph on percussion, Ralph Jones on woodwinds, Charles Moore, trumpet, flugelhorn, and Frederico Ramos, guitar...and myself. Um...now this is in, in essence its a tone poem.…
